profile.reading:
The Cable & Wireless Cable Landing Station sits at 14 Ramsey Road in Shirley, New York, on the south shore of Long Island in the town of Brookhaven. It was built by Cable & Wireless USA as the landing point for the company's own Apollo submarine cable system, a transatlantic fiber route linking the United States to the United Kingdom and France. Cable & Wireless was later absorbed into Vodafone's global network business, and the Brookhaven station passed to Vodafone along with the rest of the Apollo system's US infrastructure.

Landing stations like this one are carrier facilities rather than commercial data centers. Their job is to bring ashore the fiber pairs of a submarine cable, terminate them in line equipment, and hand traffic off to inland networks, not to host racks of customer servers. Vodafone does not publish square footage, power capacity, or tenancy details for the site, which is standard practice across the submarine cable industry for security and competitive reasons.

The Shirley area is a recognized cluster for transatlantic cable landings. AT&T operates its own Shirley landing station nearby for the TAT-12/13 and AEC-1 systems, and CenturyLink maintains separate stations at Brookhaven for the AC-1 and MAC cables and at Bellport for AC-2/Yellow, making this stretch of Long Island one of the busiest transatlantic cable corridors on the US East Coast.

reading.body:
This facility is a submarine cable landing station operated by Vodafone, not a data center campus. It terminates the Apollo transatlantic cable at Ramsey Road in Shirley, New York, and therefore functions as telecommunications infrastructure rather than compute infrastructure. No IT load capacity, power draw, or rack density is published for this location.

The station sits in New York state, where only one facility among 31 mapped data center sites has published power specifications, totaling 3 MW. This facility ranks second by published megawatts in the state, which indicates either that the single published figure in the state is below 3 MW, or that no power specification has been published for this cable station and the ranking reflects other classification. The state context provided does not clarify whether cable landing stations are included in the data center count.

For a reader assessing whether this campus matters to AI infrastructure, the answer depends on whether submarine cable capacity constrains AI at the margin. Cable landing stations enable transatlantic data transfer but do not provision compute, storage, or training capacity. This location is relevant only if international connectivity is the binding constraint on AI scaling in North America, which is not the thesis of this site.
